patient.chief_complaint: Confusion and disorientation in TIPS patient — post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy vs shunt malfunction
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H. is a 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis who underwent TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) placement 4 months ago for refractory ascites, and has been on rifaximin and lactulose prophylaxis since. His daughter (visiting from out of town) noticed he was confused and disoriented when she arrived, noting he could not remember the day, was repeating himself, and seemed 'out of it.' She was unable to reach him by phone for 3 days before arriving at his apartment. He appeared to have been eating and drinking minimally. His apartment had evidence of diarrhea — his toilet had been used repeatedly with watery stool. His daughter estimated he had 8-10 loose stools per day for the past 3-4 days. He denies alcohol use. He had recently increased his escitalopram dose from 5 mg to 10 mg one month ago. The key diagnostic question in this case: is the HE due to (1) post-TIPS HE exacerbation (common — 20-30% of TIPS patients develop HE), (2) TIPS shunt stenosis/occlusion with rebound portal hypertension causing HE, (3) lactulose overdose causing hypovolemia and electrolyte disturbance, or (4) escitalopram contributing in liver disease? Answer: lactulose overdose (8-10 stools/day) causing severe hypokalemia and hypovolemia, which in turn precipitated HE — the rifaximin is appropriate; the lactulose dose was excessive without monitoring.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, grade 2-3, post-TIPS cirrhosis — precipitated by lactulose overdose (8-10 stools/day → severe hypokalemia K 2.6 → paradoxical hyperammonemia + AKI from dehydration)

differential.key_features: Doppler shows patent shunt with normal flow velocities — shunt stenosis excluded; HE is from metabolic precipitant not shunt failure
Post-TIPS HE occurs in 20-30% of cases — correct background, but the acute precipitant is lactulose overdose; this is an exacerbation of post-TIPS HE
Escitalopram 10 mg exceeds recommended dose for Child-Pugh B (max 5 mg) — contributes to CNS depression; reduce dose but not sole cause

differential.key_features: No alcohol on toxicology; TIPS functioning — not acute decompensation from alcohol or shunt failure; lactulose overdose is the precipitant

critical_actions: Lactulose DOSE REDUCTION — paradoxical HE from lactulose overdose is a recognized phenomenon; excessive diarrhea causes hypokalemia which increases renal ammoniagenesis; target 2-3 stools/day NOT maximum diarrhea
TIPS shunt patency must be assessed — TIPS stenosis/occlusion causes recurrent ascites and HE; Doppler ultrasound required in any post-TIPS patient with HE
Hypokalemia repletion — hypokalemia is an independent HE precipitant via renal ammoniagenesis
Escitalopram dose reduction in Child-Pugh B — hepatically metabolized SSRIs accumulate; doses should be halved
contraindicated_actions: Increasing lactulose dose in response to HE — paradoxically worsens HE if overdose is the precipitant
key_reasoning_points: Lactulose overdose is an underrecognized HE precipitant — excessive diarrhea causes hypokalemia → renal ammoniagenesis → hyperammonemia → paradoxical HE worsening; always count stools/day
TIPS shunt assessment is mandatory in any post-TIPS patient with HE — shunt stenosis occurs in 25-30% within 1 year and requires revision
Post-TIPS HE occurs in 20-30% of patients and requires adjusted lactulose + rifaximin prophylaxis — dose monitoring is critical
SSRIs are hepatically metabolized — doses must be reduced in Child-Pugh B/C liver disease; escitalopram max 5 mg in hepatic impairment

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Medications listed as prescribed ≠ medications taken correctly; must ask about actual stool frequency (8-10/day → overdose); lactulose should produce 2-3 soft stools daily, not diarrhea

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all HE to expected post-TIPS encephalopathy; skip TIPS assessment; treat empirically without identifying reversible precipitant
